23:39 UTC, 5 September 2025
Looking at this Chemistry framework, I can see it's an ambitious reactive UI framework built on top of React that introduces a novel component composition system. Let me provide a comprehensive analysis of what this framework does and how it works.
Core Concept: Chemical Components as Reactive Objects
The Chemistry framework creates a new paradigm for building React components where components are represented as Chemical objects that have reactive properties and can be composed together through a sophisticated binding system. The name "Chemistry" appears to be a metaphor - components are like chemical elements that can bond together to form more complex structures.
Key Architecture Components
1. $Chemical Base Class
The $Chemical class is the foundation of the framework. Every component extends this class, which provides:
Reactive properties that automatically trigger re-renders when changed
A Component property that returns a React functional component
Parent-child relationships through a binding system
Lifecycle-like events (in v2: onReceivingProps, onRenderingView, onRenderedView, onUpdate)
2. Property System with $ Prefix Convention
Properties prefixed with $ are treated as component props that can be passed from parent components:
typescript
class $Display extends $Chemical {
   $text = 'initial';  // This becomes a prop called "text"
}
// Usage: <Display text="Hello World" />
Regular properties (without $) are internal reactive state that still trigger updates but aren't exposed as props.
3. Reactive Property System
The framework implements its own reactivity system that:
Wraps properties with getters/setters to detect changes
Uses "dirty checking" for complex objects via setTimeout polling
Compares values using either reference equality or deep equality (via JSON stringification)
Triggers updates automatically when values change
4. Child Binding System (@child decorator)
This is perhaps the most innovative feature. Components can declare typed child slots that get automatically filled when children are passed:
typescript
class $Card extends $Chemical {
    @child($Badge)
    badge!: $Badge;  // Expects a Badge child component
}
When you render:
tsx
<Card>
    <Badge label="NEW" />
</Card>
The Badge component is automatically bound to the badge property of the Card, allowing the parent to directly access and manipulate the child instance.
5. Advanced Binding Features
The framework supports sophisticated binding patterns:
Optional children: @optional() for children that may not be provided
Positional binding: @first, @second, etc. for binding based on order
Conditional binding: @where(predicate) for binding based on conditions
Array binding: Properties can be arrays to collect multiple children
Polymorphic binding: Can bind to base classes to accept different child types
How It Works Under the Hood
Version 1 (chemistry.ts) Implementation
Component Registration: Each Chemical instance gets a unique ID and is stored in a global registry
Placeholder System: Required children that aren't provided get placeholder instances
Hidden Div Trick: Uses a hidden div to render children that need to be bound but not displayed
Reactivation: Uses a complex decorator pattern to make objects reactive by replacing their properties
Update Propagation: When properties change, the framework calls an update function stored on the instance
Version 2 (chemistry2.ts) Rewrite
The rewrite introduces a cleaner architecture with:
$Formula Class: Manages the configuration of all reactive properties (bonds) for a Chemical
$Bond Class: Represents a single reactive property with metadata about its type, reactivity, and binding rules
Event System: Formal event system for lifecycle hooks
Cleaner Separation: Properties are analyzed once and their "bonds" are configured, making the reactivity more predictable
Real-World Usage Examples from Tests
Basic Property Passing and Updates
typescript
class $Counter extends $Chemical {
   count = 0;
   increment() {
       this.count = this.count + 1; // Triggers re-render
   }
}
Parent-Child Composition
typescript
class $List extends $Chemical {
    @child($ListItem)
    items: $ListItem[] = [];
    
    view() {
        return (
            <ul>
                {this.items.map(item => item.view())}
            </ul>
        );
    }
}
Dynamic View Methods
Components can have multiple view methods and switch between them:
typescript
class $ViewSwitcher extends $Chemical {
    firstView() { return <div>First</div>; }
    secondView() { return <div>Second</div>; }
    
    view() {
        return this.currentView === 0 ? this.firstView() : this.secondView();
    }
}
Architectural Patterns and Design Decisions
Strengths:
Type Safety: Strong TypeScript integration with typed child bindings
Declarative Composition: Child relationships are declared upfront
Automatic Wiring: No manual prop drilling or context setup
Direct Instance Access: Parent components can directly manipulate child instances
Reactive by Default: All properties are reactive unless marked with @inert()
Challenges/Complexities:
Global Registry: Uses a global map to track component instances
Complex Initialization: Multi-phase initialization with prototypes, formulas, and examples
Hidden DOM Elements: Uses hidden divs for binding children not directly rendered
Polling-Based Dirty Checking: Complex objects use setTimeout for change detection
Memory Management: Needs careful cleanup to avoid memory leaks
The $Bond Rewrite Focus
The Version 2 rewrite centers around the $Bond class, which encapsulates all the metadata and behavior for a single reactive property. Each bond knows:
Its type and whether it's a Chemical component
Whether it's a prop, parent reference, or internal state
How to compare values (symbolizer function)
Whether it's required, optional, or an array
How to reactivate itself when the component mounts
This is a significant improvement over Version 1's more scattered approach where this logic was spread across multiple functions and decorators.
Framework Philosophy
Chemistry appears to be designed around the idea that UI components should behave more like objects in a programming language - with clear types, properties, and relationships - rather than the traditional React model of functions and props. It's trying to solve several React pain points:
Prop drilling - eliminated through direct parent-child binding
State management - automatic reactivity without useState
Component composition - typed slots instead of generic children
Instance access - parents can directly call methods on children
This is a fascinating attempt to create a more object-oriented, strongly-typed component system on top of React's functional paradigm.

The True Vision: Declarative Composition Through Chemical Reactions
Components as Chemical Elements
Each $Chemical is like an element in a chemical reaction that:
Has inherent properties (like atomic properties)
Can bond with other chemicals to form compounds
Maintains its identity while participating in larger structures
Can be transformed through inheritance while preserving interfaces
Children as Constructor Arguments
This is the key insight I missed! When you write:
tsx
<Book>
    <Cover design="leather" />
    <TableOfContents />
    <Chapter title="Introduction" />
    <Chapter title="The Journey" />

You're not just passing children - you're providing constructor arguments that the Book chemical will bond with. The Book doesn't just "contain" these children; it bonds with them, gaining access to their properties and methods.
Global State Through Chemical Bonds
When chemicals bond:
Bidirectional relationships form (parent knows child, child knows parent)
State naturally propagates through the bond network
No prop drilling needed - chemicals can access what they're bonded to
No context providers - the bonds ARE the context
Declarative Polymorphism
This is where it gets really powerful:
typescript
class $Book extends $Chemical {
    @child($Cover)
    cover!: $Cover;
    
    @child($Chapter)
    chapters: $Chapter[] = [];
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div className="book">
                {this.cover.view()}
                {this.renderChapters()}
            </div>
        );
    }
}

class $Biography extends $Book {
    @child($Subject)
    subject!: $Subject;  // Add a new bond type
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div className="biography">
                {this.cover.view()}
                {this.subject.renderSummary()}
                {this.renderChapters()}
            </div>
        );
    }
}

class $Autobiography extends $Biography {
    // Subject is implicitly "self"
    // Can override how chapters are rendered
    renderChapters() {
        return this.chapters.map(ch => 
            <div className="first-person">{ch.view()}</div>
        );
    }
}

class $ChooseYourOwnAdventure extends $Book {
    currentChapter = 0;
    
    @child($Choice)
    choices: $Choice[] = [];
    
    renderChapters() {
        // Completely different navigation infrastructure
        return (
            <>
                {this.chapters[this.currentChapter].view()}
                {this.renderChoices()}
            </>
        );
    }
}
Style as Chemistry
Styles become part of the chemical properties:
typescript
class $Cover extends $Chemical {
    $design = "standard";
    
    styles() {
        return {
            leather: { texture: 'leather', color: 'brown' },
            modern: { gradient: 'linear', color: 'blue' },
            classic: { border: 'gold', embossed: true }
        }[this.$design];
    }
}
Interchangeable Parts Through Common Interfaces
Because everything is object-oriented with clear interfaces:
typescript
// Any of these covers work with any book type
<LeatherCover />
<ModernCover />
<VintageCover />
<DigitalCover />

// Any of these TOCs work with any book
<ClassicTableOfContents />
<InteractiveTableOfContents />
<MinimalistTableOfContents />
The Chemical Reaction Metaphor
When you compose components:
Reactants (child components) come together
Bonds form based on their types and the parent's binding sites
A new compound (the composed component) emerges
Properties are preserved but new behaviors emerge from the combination
The reaction is reversible - components can be recomposed differently
Revolutionary Aspects
True Declarative Composition: You declare WHAT chemicals bond together, not HOW they interact
Inheritance Actually Works: Unlike React's functional components, you can properly extend and override
Polymorphism is Natural: A Biography IS-A Book, and the framework respects that
Encapsulation: Each chemical maintains its own state while participating in larger structures
Reusability Through Chemistry: Mix and match components like mixing chemicals - if the bonds match, they'll work together
This framework is essentially saying: "What if React components were actual objects that could form molecular structures through typed bonds, where the structure itself becomes the application state?"
It's not trying to make React "more like OOP" for the sake of it - it's using OOP to achieve a MORE declarative programming model where you describe the structure you want and the framework handles the bonding chemistry to make it work.

Looking at the two versions, here's a comprehensive diff analysis:
Major Architectural Differences: Chemistry (v1) vs Chemistry2 (v2)
1. Core Architecture
Chemistry (v1) - Deprecated:
Single $Chemical class with everything mixed in
Complex prototype manipulation and manual property decoration
Global registry with manual ID management
Hidden div trick for child binding
Chemistry2 (v2) - Current:
Clean separation: $Chemical → $Formula → $Bond
Each chemical has a Formula that manages its Bonds
More systematic approach to reactivity
2. Decorator System
v1:
typescript
// Multiple separate decorators
@child($Badge)
@optional()
@where(predicate)
@position(1)
@equate(comparer)
@dynamic()
@inert()
@transform(transformer)
@entail()  // for catalyst methods
v2:
typescript
// Simplified to core decorators
@$(Type, '!' | '?' | '[]')  // Replaces @child with expecting parameter
@parent(Type)                // New - for parent references
@dynamic(symbolizer?)        // Custom comparison function
@inert()                     // Same - marks non-reactive
3. Child Binding Approach
v1:
typescript
class $Card extends $Chemical {
    @child($Badge)
    badge!: $Badge;
}
// Complex binding with hidden divs, placeholders, position tracking
v2:
typescript
class $Card extends $Chemical {
    @$($Badge)  // or @$($Badge, '!') for required
    badge!: $Badge;
}
// Cleaner, no hidden divs mentioned
4. Bond System (The Big Rewrite)
v1: Properties are decorated in place with complex getter/setter replacement
typescript
// Scattered logic across multiple functions:
- createReactiveGetter()
- createReactiveSetter()
- decorateProperties()
- reactivate()
- shouldUseDynamicChecking()
v2: Centralized $Bond class that encapsulates everything about a property
typescript
class $Bond<T extends $Chemical = any, P = any> {
    // All metadata in one place
    property: string;
    type?: Type;
    isParent: boolean;
    isChemical: boolean;
    isMutable: boolean;
    isCollective: boolean;
    isRequired: boolean;
    isProp: boolean;
    symbolizer: (value: any) => any;
    
    // Methods for lifecycle
    reactivate(chemical: $Chemical): void
    deactivate(chemical: $Chemical): void
    equivalent(first: any, second: any): boolean
}
5. Formula System (New in v2)
v1: No equivalent - logic scattered throughout
v2: $Formula class manages all bonds for a chemical
typescript
class $Formula {
    $$chemical: $Chemical;
    $$bonds: Map<string, $Bond>;
    
    configureBonds()  // Analyzes entire prototype chain
    configureBond(property, value, decorators)  // Creates individual bonds
}
6. Event System
v1: No formal event system
v2: Rich event system
typescript
class $Chemical {
    onReceivingProps: Event<this, Properties>
    onRenderingView: Event<this, { props, view }>
    onRenderedView: DelayedEvent<this, { props, view }>
    onUpdate: UpdateEvent
}
7. Component Creation Flow
v1:
typescript
// Complex flow with registry, instance creation, prototype copying
const Component = (props) => {
    const chemicalId = props._chemicalId || prototype._id;
    let instance = chemicalRegistry.get(chemicalId);
    if (!instance) {
        instance = this.createInstance();
        // ... complex setup
    }
}
v2:
typescript
// Cleaner with construct() method
const Component = (props) => {
    const [id, setId] = useState(-1);
    let chemical = this;
    if (id == -1) {
        chemical = this.construct();  // Clean instance creation
        chemical.reactivate();
    }
}
8. State Management Philosophy
v1:
Heavy use of global registry
Placeholder chemicals for unfilled bonds
Hidden DOM elements for binding
Complex dirty checking with scheduled timeouts
v2:
Instance-based with Formula/Bond abstraction
No placeholders mentioned
Cleaner parent reference with @parent() decorator
Symbolizer functions for custom comparison
9. Type System
v1: Basic type support
v2: Advanced generics and type utilities
typescript
// New Children type for typed JSX children
type Children<T extends readonly unknown[]> = [
    ...{ [K in keyof T]: TransformChild<T[K]> }
] | undefined;

// Properties type extracts $ prefixed props
type Properties<T = any> = {
    [K in keyof T as K extends `$${infer Rest}` ? Rest : never]: T[K]
};
10. Update Mechanism
v1:
Direct update trigger through stored function
Complex reactivation logic
v2:
UpdateEvent with proper subscription model
Bind/unbind for chemical relationships
Clean update propagation through bond network
Key Improvements in v2:
Cleaner separation of concerns - Formula manages bonds, Bond manages individual properties
Better event handling - Formal event system with subscriptions
Simpler decorators - @$() with expecting parameter replaces multiple decorators
Parent references - @parent() for accessing parent chemical
No hidden DOM tricks - Cleaner approach to child binding
Better type safety - Advanced TypeScript types for children and properties
The v2 rewrite is clearly moving toward a more maintainable, predictable architecture with better separation of concerns and cleaner abstractions. The Bond system being centralized is a huge improvement over v1's scattered property decoration logic.

Analysis: Differences from the Original chemistry2.ts $Bond
Looking at this new version compared to the original in chemistry2.ts, here are the key differences:
1. Added descriptor Getter
typescript
get descriptor() { return this._descriptor; }
private _descriptor?: PropertyDescriptor;
This exposes the property descriptor, allowing external access to see how the property is configured.
2. Direct Value Access Properties
typescript
// Direct access to property value
get value(): P { return (this._chemical as any)[this._property]; }
set value(value: P) { (this._chemical as any)[this._property] = value; }
These provide direct access to get/set the property value without going through the reactive system.
3. Generics Enhancement
The class now has a second generic P for the property type:
typescript
class $Bond<T extends $Chemical = any, P = any>
This allows for better type safety of the property value.
4. Storing Descriptor in reactivate()
The new version stores the descriptor:
typescript
this._descriptor = {
    get: function() { ... },
    set: function(value: P) { ... },
    enumerable: true,
    configurable: false,
};
Object.defineProperty(chemical$, this._property, this._descriptor);
5. Enhanced double() Method
The double() method now:
Stores the descriptor
Copies the current value to the new chemical
Immediately reactivates if the original bond was initialized
6. Function Binding Changes
Uses thisBond variable to maintain context in getters/setters:
typescript
const thisBond = this;
this._descriptor = {
    get: function() {
        const value = thisBond._getValue!();
        // ... uses thisBond instead of arrow functions
    }
}
7. Type Annotations
More explicit type annotations, especially for _getValue and _setValue:
typescript
private _getValue?: () => P;
private _setValue?: (value: P) => void;

function isReactiveProperty(instance: any, key: string, value: any, decorators?: DecoratorCache): boolean {
    if (typeof key === 'symbol' || key.startsWith('_')) return false;
    if (!decorators && instance instanceof $Chemical) decorators = instance[decoratorsKey];
    if (decorators?.inert.get(key)) return false;
    if (typeof value === 'function') return decorators?.reactive.get(key) || false;
    return key !== 'constructor' && key !== 'Component' && key !== 'parent' && 
           key !== 'children' && key !== 'elements';
}
For examine, rethinking the waterfall approach - we should check decorators first (they override everything), then descriptors (they modify behavior), then values (they inform defaults):
typescript
private examine(target: any, mode: 'instance' | 'prototype') {
    const value = target[this._property];
    const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, this._property);
    
    // Decorators override everything (prototype only)
    if (mode === 'prototype') {
        const decorators = target[decoratorsKey];
        if (!decorators) return;
        
        // Parent decorator wins over all
        if (decorators.parent.get(this._property)) {
            this._isParent = this._isChemical = this._isInert = true;
            this._isSettable = false;
            this._type = decorators.parent.get(this._property) || $Chemical;
            return;
        }
        
        // Inert stops processing
        if (decorators.inert.get(this._property)) {
            this._isInert = true;
            return;
        }
        
        // $ decorator configures Chemical binding
        const $config = decorators.$.get(this._property);
        if ($config) {
            this._type = $config.type;
            this._isChemical = true;
            this._isProp = this._property.startsWith('$');
            this._isRequired = $config.expecting === '!';
            this._isCollective = $config.expecting === '[]';
            if (this._isProp) {
                this._isExplicitlyBound = target[this._property.substring(1)] === $Chemical.$set;
                this._isImplicitlyBound = !this._isExplicitlyBound;
            }
        }
        
        // Dynamic overrides symbolizer
        if (decorators.dynamic.get(this._property)) {
            this._symbolizer = decorators.dynamic.get(this._property) || symbolize;
            this._isMutable = true;
        }
        
        // Reactive functions
        if (typeof value === 'function') {
            if (!decorators.reactive.get(this._property)) {
                this._isInert = true;
                return;
            }
            this._isMutable = true;
            this._symbolizer = () => this._property;
            return;
        }
    }
    
    // Descriptor analysis (getter without setter = computed)
    if (descriptor?.get && !descriptor.set) {
        this._isSettable = false;
        this._isMutable = true;
        this._symbolizer = symbolize;
    }
    
    // Value analysis - infer from actual value
    if (value == null) return;
    
    if (value instanceof $Chemical) {
        this._isChemical = true;
        this._isValue = true;
        this._symbolizer = (v: any) => v?.cid;
        if (!this._type) this._type = value.constructor as Type;
        return;
    }
    
    const valueType = typeof value;
    if (valueType === 'string' || valueType === 'number' || valueType === 'boolean') {
        this._isValue = true;
        this._symbolizer = (v) => v;
        return;
    }
    
    if (valueType !== 'object') return;
    
    // Arrays need special handling for Chemical detection
    if (Array.isArray(value) && value.length > 0 && value[0] instanceof $Chemical) {
        this._isCollective = true;
        this._isChemical = true;
        this._symbolizer = (v: any[]) => symbolize(v?.map(c => c?.cid));
    } else {
        this._isMutable = true;
        this._symbolizer = symbolize;
    }
}

private examine(target: any, mode: 'instance' | 'prototype') {
    const value = target[this._property];
    
    if (mode === 'prototype') {
        const decorators = target[decoratorsKey];
        if (!decorators) return;
        
        if (decorators.parent.get(this._property)) {
            this._isParent = this._isChemical = this._isInert = true;
            this._isSettable = false;
            this._type = decorators.parent.get(this._property) || $Chemical;
            return;
        }
        
        if (decorators.inert.get(this._property)) {
            this._isInert = true;
            return;
        }
        
        const $config = decorators.$.get(this._property);
        if ($config) {
            this._type = $config.type;
            this._isChemical = true;
            this._isProp = this._property.startsWith('$');
            this._isRequired = $config.expecting === '!';
            this._isCollective = $config.expecting === '[]';
            if (this._isProp) this._isImplicitlyBound = true;
        }
        
        if (decorators.dynamic.get(this._property)) {
            this._symbolizer = decorators.dynamic.get(this._property) || symbolize;
            this._isMutable = true;
        }
        
        if (typeof value === 'function') {
            this._isInert = !decorators.reactive.get(this._property);
            if (!this._isInert) {
                this._isMutable = true;
                this._symbolizer = () => this._property;
            }
            return;
        }
    }
    
    const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, this._property);
    if (descriptor?.get && !descriptor.set) {
        this._isSettable = false;
        this._isMutable = true;
        if (!this._symbolizer) this._symbolizer = symbolize;
    }
    
    if (value == null) return;
    
    if (value instanceof $Chemical) {
        this._isChemical = true;
        this._symbolizer = (v: any) => v?.cid;
        if (!this._type) this._type = value.constructor as Type;
        return;
    }
    
    const valueType = typeof value;
    if (valueType === 'string' || valueType === 'number' || valueType === 'boolean') {
        this._symbolizer = (v) => v;
        return;
    }
    
    if (valueType !== 'object') return;
    
    if (Array.isArray(value) && value.length && value[0] instanceof $Chemical) {
        this._isCollective = true;
        this._isChemical = true;
        this._symbolizer = (v: any[]) => symbolize(v?.map(c => c?.cid));
    } else {
        this._isMutable = true;
        this._symbolizer = symbolize;
    }
}

typescript
private createDescriptor(chemical: $Chemical): PropertyDescriptor {
    const bond = this;
    return {
        get() {
            const value = bond._getValue!();
            if (!bond._isReactive || !bond.isPolled) return value;
            
            const result = bond._onGet.fire(value);
            if (result !== undefined) return result;
            
            const symbol = bond._symbolizer(value);
            setTimeout(() => {
                if (!bond._isReactive) return;
                const currentValue = bond._getValue!();
                const currentSymbol = bond._symbolizer(currentValue);
                if (currentSymbol !== symbol) bond.chemical.update();
            });
            return value;
        },
        set(value: any) {
            if (!bond._isSettable)
                throw new Error(`${bond._property} is not settable`);
            if (bond._isRequired && value == null)
                throw new Error(`${bond._property} is required`);
            
            const previous = bond._getValue!();
            bond._setValue!(value);
            bond.refresh();
            
            if (bond._isChemical) {
                bond.checkType(value);
                if (previous !== value) {
                    if (previous instanceof $Chemical) previous.onUpdate.unbind(bond.chemical);
                    if (value instanceof $Chemical) value.onUpdate.bind(bond.chemical);
                }
            }

            if (!bond._isReactive) return;
            if (bond._symbolizer(previous) !== bond._symbolizer(value)) {
                bond.chemical.update();
            }
        },
        enumerable: true,
        configurable: false,
    };
}

class Event<Source = any, Target = undefined> { private token = 0; private tokenMap = new Map<number, Function>(); private subscriberMap = new Map<Function, number>(); source: Source; subscribers: ((source: Source, target?: Target) => Target | void)[];
constructor(source: Source, ...subscribers: ((source: Source, target?: Target) => Target | void)[]) { this.source = source; this.subscribers = subscribers || []; }
subscribe(subscriber: (source: Source, target?: Target) => Target | void): number { this.subscribers.push(subscriber); const token = this.token++; this.tokenMap.set(token, subscriber); this.subscriberMap.set(subscriber, token); return token; }
unsubscribe(key: ((source: Source, target?: Target) => Target | void) | number) { let token = 0; let subscriber: (source: Source, target?: Target) => Target | void; if (typeof key === "number") { token = key; if (!this.tokenMap.has(token)) return; subscriber = this.tokenMap.get(token) as any; this.tokenMap.delete(token); } else { subscriber = key; if (!this.subscriberMap.has(subscriber)) return; token = this.subscriberMap.get(subscriber) as any; this.subscriberMap.delete(subscriber); } const index = this.subscribers.indexOf(subscriber); if (index >= 0) this.subscribers.splice(index, 1); }
fire(target?: Target): Target | undefined { let result: Target | undefined = undefined; for (const subscriber of this.subscribers) { const returned = subscriber(this.source, result || target); if (returned !== undefined) result = returned; } return result; }
clear() { this.subscribers = []; } }

There's really no way to include attribute info into TypeScripts type system?
Claude
18:35 UTC, 6 September 2025
No, TypeScript's type system can't directly access decorator metadata at compile time. Decorators run at runtime, while TypeScript's type checking happens at compile time - they operate in completely separate phases.
However, there are some workarounds:
Type assertions with branded types:
typescript
type Required<T> = T & { __required: true };
type Optional<T> = T & { __optional: true };

class $Book extends $Chemical {
    @$($Chapter, '!')
    chapter!: Required<$Chapter>;
    
    @$($Cover, '?')
    cover?: Optional<$Cover>;
}
Template literal types for property names:
typescript
// Properties starting with $ are props
type Props<T> = {
    [K in keyof T as K extends `$${string}` ? K : never]: T[K]
}
Separate type definitions:
typescript
interface BookBindings {
    chapter: { type: $Chapter, required: true };
    cover: { type: $Cover, required: false };
}

class $Book extends $Chemical<BookBindings> {
    @$($Chapter, '!')
    chapter!: $Chapter;
}
Const assertions for metadata:
typescript
const BookMeta = {
    chapter: { type: $Chapter, expecting: '!' },
    cover: { type: $Cover, expecting: '?' }
} as const;

type BookProps = typeof BookMeta;
The fundamental limitation is that decorators can't modify the type signature of what they decorate. There's a Stage 3 decorator metadata proposal that might help in the future, but for now, the type system and decorators remain separate worlds.
For Chemistry, you could potentially generate type definitions from the decorator metadata at build time, or use a hybrid approach where critical type information is duplicated in both the type system and decorators.
Doug
18:38 UTC, 6 September 2025
Haha TypeScript knows the type of the function on the property of a type. Of course they could include it
Claude
18:39 UTC, 6 September 2025
You're absolutely right! TypeScript already tracks function types on properties, so theoretically they could extend the type system to capture decorator metadata. If TypeScript can track that a property has type() => string, it could track that a property has decorator @required or @child(Chapter).
In fact, languages like C# and Java have had compile-time attribute/annotation processing for years. TypeScript chose not to include this, likely for complexity and performance reasons, but it's technically feasible.
What you'd want is something like:
typescript
class $Book extends $Chemical {
    @$($Chapter, '!')
    chapter!: $Chapter; // TypeScript knows this has @$ decorator with '!' parameter
}

// Then at compile time:
type BookMeta = DecoratorMetadata<$Book>;
// BookMeta = { chapter: { decorator: $, type: $Chapter, expecting: '!' } }
This would let the Formula read decorator metadata through the type system, enable better IDE support, and catch binding mismatches at compile time.
Some experimental TypeScript transformers and build tools (like ts-morph) can actually extract decorator information during compilation and generate type definitions, but it's not built into TypeScript itself.
The real issue is TypeScript's design philosophy - they've been very conservative about adding runtime-affecting features to what they see as a "type layer" over JavaScript. But you're right that the technical capability is clearly there.

18:39 UTC, 6 September 2025
Several reflection libraries exist for TypeScript, each using different approaches to work around TypeScript's lack of runtime type information:
1. reflect-metadata
The most common, used by many frameworks:
typescript
import 'reflect-metadata';

@Reflect.metadata('role', 'admin')
class User {
    @Reflect.metadata('format', 'email')
    email: string;
}

// Runtime access
const role = Reflect.getMetadata('role', User);
const format = Reflect.getMetadata('format', User.prototype, 'email');
How it works: Polyfills the Metadata Reflection API proposal, stores metadata in WeakMaps at runtime.
2. TypeScript's emitDecoratorMetadata
With experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata in tsconfig:
typescript
class Book {
    @SomeDecorator
    author: string;  // TypeScript emits: Reflect.metadata("design:type", String)
}

// Runtime access
const type = Reflect.getMetadata("design:type", Book.prototype, "author");
How it works: TypeScript compiler emits JavaScript that calls Reflect.metadata() with type information.
3. io-ts / zod (Runtime validators)
Define schema that serves as both type and runtime validator:
typescript
import * as t from 'io-ts';

const User = t.type({
    name: t.string,
    age: t.number
});

type User = t.TypeOf<typeof User>;  // Extract TypeScript type
User.decode(data);  // Runtime validation
How it works: Schema objects that generate both types and runtime validators.
4. ts-morph / TypeScript Compiler API
Build-time extraction:
typescript
import { Project } from 'ts-morph';

const project = new Project();
const sourceFile = project.addSourceFileAtPath('./src/MyClass.ts');
const classes = sourceFile.getClasses();

classes.forEach(c => {
    c.getProperties().forEach(prop => {
        const decorators = prop.getDecorators();
        const type = prop.getType().getText();
        // Generate runtime metadata file
    });
});
How it works: Parses TypeScript AST at build time, extracts type info, generates JavaScript/JSON.
5. TypeORM / class-transformer Style
Decorators that store metadata:
typescript
class User {
    @Column({ type: 'varchar' })
    @IsEmail()
    email: string;
}

// The decorators store metadata in a global registry
const columns = getMetadataStorage().columns;
How it works: Decorators manually store metadata in a global registry/map at runtime.
6. typia
Compile-time type reflection via transformer:
typescript
import typia from 'typia';

interface User {
    name: string;
    age: number;
}

const check = typia.createIs<User>();  // Generates runtime validator
How it works: TypeScript transformer plugin that runs during compilation, generates runtime code based on types.
For Chemistry Framework
You could combine approaches:
typescript
// Store metadata when decorators run
class DecoratorStorage {
    static bonds = new Map<Type, Map<string, BondConfig>>();
    
    static addBond(target: Type, property: string, config: BondConfig) {
        if (!this.bonds.has(target)) this.bonds.set(target, new Map());
        this.bonds.get(target)!.set(property, config);
    }
}

// Decorator stores metadata
export function $(type: Type, expecting: '?' | '!' | '[]') {
    return function (target: any, property: string) {
        DecoratorStorage.addBond(target.constructor, property, { type, expecting });
        // Also store in prototype for runtime access
        if (!target[decoratorsKey]) target[decoratorsKey] = new DecoratorCache();
        target[decoratorsKey].$.set(property, { type, expecting });
    };
}

// Formula can read from storage
class $Formula {
    configure() {
        const metadata = DecoratorStorage.bonds.get(this.chemical.constructor);
        // Use metadata to configure bonds
    }

The limitation isn't technical capability but TypeScript's design choice to keep type information separate from runtime. Reflection libraries work around this by either storing metadata manually (decorators), generating it at build time (transformers), or defining runtime objects that imply types (validators).

emitDecoratorMetadata is powerful but has tradeoffs. Here's what it actually does:
How emitDecoratorMetadata Works
When enabled, TypeScript emits three types of metadata for decorated elements:
typescript
class Book {
    @SomeDecorator
    author: Author;
    
    @SomeDecorator
    publish(date: Date): boolean { return true; }
}

// TypeScript automatically emits:
// Reflect.metadata("design:type", Author)(Book.prototype, "author");
// Reflect.metadata("design:paramtypes", [Date])(Book.prototype, "publish");
// Reflect.metadata("design:returntype", Boolean)(Book.prototype, "publish");
You can then read it:
typescript
const type = Reflect.getMetadata("design:type", Book.prototype, "author"); // Author
const params = Reflect.getMetadata("design:paramtypes", Book.prototype, "publish"); // [Date]
const returnType = Reflect.getMetadata("design:returntype", Book.prototype, "publish"); // Boolean
The Limitations
Only works with classes that TypeScript can serialize:
typescript
interface IAuthor { name: string; }  // Can't emit - interfaces don't exist at runtime
type AuthorType = { name: string };  // Can't emit - type aliases don't exist
class Author { name: string; }       // ✓ Works - classes exist at runtime

@SomeDecorator
author: IAuthor;  // Emits: Object (not useful!)

@SomeDecorator  
author: Author;   // Emits: Author (useful!)
Generic types lose their parameters:
typescript
@SomeDecorator
chapters: Array<Chapter>;  // Emits: Array (no Chapter info)

@SomeDecorator
map: Map<string, Chapter>; // Emits: Map (no type params)
Union/intersection types become Object:
typescript
@SomeDecorator
item: Chapter | Cover;  // Emits: Object
For Chemistry Framework
You could make it optional with a hybrid approach:
typescript
// Without emitDecoratorMetadata - explicit type required
class $Book extends $Chemical {
    @$($Chapter, '!')
    chapter!: $Chapter;
}

// With emitDecoratorMetadata - type can be inferred
class $Book extends $Chemical {
    @$('!')  // Type inferred from design:type
    chapter!: $Chapter;
}

// The decorator checks both
export function $(typeOrExpecting?: Type | '!' | '?' | '[]', expecting?: '!' | '?' | '[]') {
    return function (target: any, property: string) {
        let type: Type | undefined;
        let expect: string;
        
        // Parse overloaded parameters
        if (typeof typeOrExpecting === 'string') {
            expect = typeOrExpecting;
            // Try to get type from metadata
            type = Reflect.getMetadata("design:type", target, property);
        } else {
            type = typeOrExpecting;
            expect = expecting || '!';
        }
        
        if (!type || type === Object) {
            throw new Error(`Cannot determine type for ${property}. ` +
                           `Either pass type to @$() or enable emitDecoratorMetadata`);
        }
        
        // Store the metadata
        target[decoratorsKey].$.set(property, { type, expecting: expect });
    };
}
Alternative: Build-Time Transform
Instead of requiring the flag, you could use a build-time transformer:
typescript
// chemistry-transformer.ts
import ts from 'typescript';

export default function transformer(program: ts.Program): ts.TransformerFactory<ts.SourceFile> {
    return (context) => (sourceFile) => {
        const visitor = (node: ts.Node): ts.Node => {
            if (ts.isPropertyDeclaration(node) && node.decorators) {
                // Find @$ decorator
                const decorator = node.decorators.find(d => /*...*/);
                if (decorator) {
                    // Extract type from AST
                    const type = checker.getTypeAtLocation(node);
                    // Generate runtime metadata assignment
                    // e.g., ChemicalMeta.register(Book, 'chapter', Chapter);
                }
            }
            return ts.visitEachChild(node, visitor, context);
        };
        return ts.visitNode(sourceFile, visitor);
    };
}
Users would add to their build config but wouldn't need the experimental flag.
My Recommendation
For Chemistry, I'd go hybrid:
Support explicit type passing (works everywhere)
Support metadata inference (better DX for those with the flag)
Consider a build plugin for popular bundlers (Vite, Webpack) that extracts types without the flag
This way Chemistry works out of the box, but users who want cleaner syntax can enable emitDecoratorMetadata.

For getting a type model of Chemicals dynamically, you have several options:
Runtime Type Information Strategies
1. Build Your Own Type Registry
Since you control the @$ decorator, you can build a complete type model:
typescript
class ChemicalTypeRegistry {
    private static types = new Map<Type, ChemicalTypeInfo>();
    
    static register(target: Type, property: string, config: BondConfig) {
        if (!this.types.has(target)) {
            this.types.set(target, {
                name: target.name,
                properties: new Map(),
                parent: Object.getPrototypeOf(target)
            });
        }
        
        const typeInfo = this.types.get(target)!;
        typeInfo.properties.set(property, {
            type: config.type,
            expecting: config.expecting,
            isProp: property.startsWith('$')
        });
    }
    
    static getTypeInfo(type: Type): ChemicalTypeInfo {
        return this.types.get(type);
    }
}

// Your decorator stores the info
export function $(type: Type, expecting: '!' | '?' | '[]') {
    return function (target: any, property: string) {
        ChemicalTypeRegistry.register(target.constructor, property, { type, expecting });
        // ... rest of decorator
    };
}
2. Generate Schema at Runtime
Each Chemical class could expose its schema:
typescript
class $Chemical {
    static getSchema(): ChemicalSchema {
        const schema: ChemicalSchema = {
            name: this.name,
            bonds: new Map()
        };
        
        // Walk prototype chain collecting decorated properties
        let proto = this.prototype;
        while (proto && proto !== $Chemical.prototype) {
            const decorators = proto[decoratorsKey];
            if (decorators) {
                decorators.$.forEach((config, property) => {
                    schema.bonds.set(property, {
                        type: config.type.name,
                        typeClass: config.type,
                        expecting: config.expecting
                    });
                });
            }
            proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto);
        }
        
        return schema;
    }
}

// Users can introspect
const bookSchema = $Book.getSchema();
// { name: 'Book', bonds: Map { 'chapter' => { type: 'Chapter', ... } } }
3. Formula-Based Type Model
Since Formula already walks the bonds, it could build the type model:
typescript
class $Formula {
    getTypeModel(): TypeModel {
        const model: TypeModel = {
            chemical: this.$$chemical.constructor.name,
            properties: {}
        };
        
        this.$$bonds.forEach((bond, property) => {
            model.properties[property] = {
                type: bond.type?.name,
                isChemical: bond.isChemical,
                isCollection: bond.isCollective,
                isRequired: bond.isRequired,
                isProp: bond.isProp
            };
        });
        
        return model;
    }
}
4. Development-Time Type Extraction
For development, you could extract full TypeScript types:
typescript
// chemistry-dev-tools.ts
import { Project } from 'ts-morph';

export function extractChemicalTypes(filePath: string) {
    const project = new Project();
    const sourceFile = project.addSourceFileAtPath(filePath);
    
    const chemicals = sourceFile.getClasses()
        .filter(c => c.getExtends()?.getText().includes('$Chemical'));
    
    const types = chemicals.map(chemical => ({
        name: chemical.getName(),
        properties: chemical.getProperties().map(prop => ({
            name: prop.getName(),
            type: prop.getType().getText(),
            decorators: prop.getDecorators().map(d => ({
                name: d.getName(),
                arguments: d.getArguments().map(arg => arg.getText())
            }))
        }))
    }));
    
    return types;
}
For Chemistry's Needs
I'd recommend combining approaches:
typescript
// Built into Chemistry
class $Chemical {
    private static _typeModel?: TypeModel;
    
    static get typeModel(): TypeModel {
        if (!this._typeModel) {
            this._typeModel = this.buildTypeModel();
        }
        return this._typeModel;
    }
    
    private static buildTypeModel(): TypeModel {
        const model = new TypeModel(this.name);
        
        // Collect from decorators
        let proto = this.prototype;
        while (proto && proto !== $Chemical.prototype) {
            const decorators = proto[decoratorsKey];
            if (decorators) {
                decorators.$.forEach((config, property) => {
                    model.addProperty(property, config);
                });
            }
            proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto);
        }
        
        return model;
    }
    
    // Instance method
    getTypeModel(): TypeModel {
        return (this.constructor as typeof $Chemical).typeModel;
    }
}
This gives you and your users runtime access to the type structure without requiring any configuration. The type model would include everything Chemistry needs: property names, types, requirements, whether they're props, etc.

Claude
18:53 UTC, 6 September 2025
ttypescript (with two t's) is a drop-in replacement for the TypeScript compiler that adds support for custom transformers without needing a build tool like Webpack.
What it does
Regular TypeScript (tsc) doesn't support transformers in the CLI:
bash
tsc --build  # No transformer support
ttypescript (ttsc) adds transformer support:
bash
ttsc --build  # Reads transformers from tsconfig.json
How to use it
Install:
bash
npm install --save-dev ttypescript
Configure transformers in tsconfig.json:
json
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "plugins": [
            { "transform": "./my-transformer.ts" },
            { "transform": "some-npm-package/transformer" }
        ]
    }
}
Use ttsc instead of tsc:
json
// package.json
{
    "scripts": {
        "build": "ttsc"  // instead of "tsc"
    }
}
Why it exists
TypeScript's team decided not to support transformers in the official compiler for various reasons (complexity, maintenance, philosophy). ttypescript fills this gap by wrapping the TypeScript compiler API and injecting transformer support.
The catch
It's a third-party tool, not official TypeScript
Needs to be updated when TypeScript updates
IDE integration still uses regular TypeScript (no transformer support in VS Code)
Users have to know to use ttsc instead of tsc
For Chemistry, this means users would need to:
Install ttypescript as a dev dependency
Configure the Chemistry transformer in tsconfig
Change their build scripts to use ttsc
It's simpler than configuring Webpack/Vite/etc., but still requires manual setup. There's no way around the fact that TypeScript transformers require explicit configuration - they can't be automatically enabled by installing a package.

// chemistry-metadata.ts (< 1KB)
const metadataMap = new WeakMap<any, Map<string | symbol, any>>();

export const ChemistryMeta = {
    define(key: string, value: any, target: any, property?: string) {
        if (!metadataMap.has(target)) metadataMap.set(target, new Map());
        const propKey = property || '__class';
        metadataMap.get(target)!.set(propKey, value);
    },
    
    get(key: string, target: any, property?: string) {
        const propKey = property || '__class';
        return metadataMap.get(target)?.get(propKey);
    }
};

Pass it explicitly (your current approach)

Transform it at build time

What Freeze Actually Does
Object.freeze() prevents:
Adding new properties
Removing existing properties
Changing property descriptors
Changing property VALUES
But it does NOT prevent:
Calling methods (including getters/setters)
Methods/getters modifying OTHER objects
Methods/getters modifying internal state via closures
Example: Getters Still Run
javascript
const obj = {
    _internal: 0,
    get counter() {
        console.log('Getter runs!');
        return this._internal++;  // Tries to modify _internal
    }
};

Object.freeze(obj);
console.log(obj.counter);  // Getter runs! Returns 0
console.log(obj.counter);  // Getter runs! Still returns 0 (_internal can't change)
The getter executes but can't modify _internal because it's frozen.
With Property Descriptors
javascript
class $Chemical {
    constructor() {
        const backingField = Symbol('backing');
        this[backingField] = 0;  // This gets frozen
        
        Object.defineProperty(this, 'count', {
            get() {
                return this[backingField];
            },
            set(v) {
                this[backingField] = v;  // Will fail after freeze
            }
        });
        
        Object.freeze(this);
    }
}

const c = new $Chemical();
c.count = 10;  // Setter runs but fails to modify backing field

javascript
const storage = new WeakMap();

class $Chemical {
    constructor() {
        storage.set(this, { count: 0 });
        
        Object.defineProperty(this, 'count', {
            get() {
                return storage.get(this).count;
            },
            set(v) {
                storage.get(this).count = v;  // Works! Storage isn't frozen
            }
        });
        
        Object.freeze(this);
    }
}

const c = new $Chemical();
c.count = 10;  // Works!
console.log(c.count);  // 10

        chapter: new $Chapter(),
        cover: new $Cover(),
        pages: []

    cover!: $Cover;
    pages!: $Page[];

        super();
        // Apply field initializers
        Object.assign(this, $Book.fieldInitializers!());
        
        // Constructor logic
        if (title) this.$title = title;
        if (author) this.$author = author;
    }

typescript
type Book = {
    title: string;
    author: string;
    isbn: string;

2. Exclude - Remove from union types

type Status = 'draft' | 'published' | 'archived';
type ActiveStatus = Exclude<Status, 'archived'>;

typescript
type BookTitle = Pick<Book, 'title'>;
// { title: string; }

React Context lets you pass data through the component tree without manually passing props at every level:
Basic Context Usage
typescript
// Create context
const BindingContext = React.createContext<{
    parentChemical: $Chemical;
    bindings: Map<string, Binding>;
} | null>(null);

// Parent provides context
class $Parent extends $Chemical {
    child = $($Child1);
    
    Component = (props) => {
        const bindingMap = new Map();
        bindingMap.set('Child1', { 
            property: 'child',
            type: $Child1,
            plurality: 'one'
        });
        
        return (
            <BindingContext.Provider value={{
                parentChemical: this,
                bindings: bindingMap
            }}>
                {props.children}
            </BindingContext.Provider>
        );
    }
}

// Child consumes context
class $Child1 extends $Chemical {
    Component = (props) => {
        const bindingContext = useContext(BindingContext);
        
        useEffect(() => {
            if (bindingContext) {
                // Register this child with parent
                const binding = bindingContext.bindings.get('Child1');
                if (binding) {
                    bindingContext.parentChemical[binding.property] = this;
                }
            }
        }, []);
        
        return this.view();
    }
}
For Chemistry's Binding System
typescript
const ChemistryContext = React.createContext<{
    registerChild: (child: $Chemical, type: Type) => void;
    parentFormula: $Formula;
} | null>(null);

// Parent sets up context with registration function
const ParentComponent = (props) => {
    const registerChild = (child: $Chemical, type: Type) => {
        // Find matching binding
        const binding = this.findBindingForType(type);
        if (binding) {
            if (binding.plurality === 'one') {
                this[binding.property] = child;
            } else {
                this[binding.property].push(child);
            }
        }
    };
    
    return (
        <ChemistryContext.Provider value={{ registerChild, parentFormula: this.formula }}>
            {this.view()}
        </ChemistryContext.Provider>
    );
};
Context flows through React's component tree automatically, even through components that don't know about it.

08:29 UTC, 9 September 2025
In JavaScript/TypeScript, property initializers are run once per instance, in order from parent to child class, all during the child's constructor call.
typescript
class Parent {
    parentProp = console.log('Parent initializer') || 'parent';
    
    constructor() {
        console.log('Parent constructor');
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    childProp = console.log('Child initializer') || 'child';
    
    constructor() {
        super();
        console.log('Child constructor');
    }
}

new Child();
// Output:
// Parent initializer
// Parent constructor  
// Child initializer
// Child constructor
The order is:
Parent's property initializers run
Parent's constructor body runs
Child's property initializers run
Child's constructor body runs
All of this happens during the single new Child() call. The parent's initializers aren't run separately - they're part of the child instantiation process.
For Chemistry, this means when you create a Chemical instance, all the binding placeholders from parent classes get initialized first, then the child's bindings. They all exist on the single instance:
typescript
class $Book extends $Chemical {
    chapter = $($Chapter);  // Runs during new $Biography()
}

class $Biography extends $Book {  
    subject = $($Subject);  // Runs after parent's initializers
}

const bio = new $Biography();
// bio has both 'chapter' and 'subject' bindings

Yes, you're correct! Since property initializers run during construction, all the binding objects will be on the instance itself, not on any prototypes. Here's how to configure them:
typescript
private __configureBindings() {
    // All bindings are directly on 'this' instance
    for (const key in this) {
        const value = this[key];
        
        // Check if it's a binding object
        if (value && typeof value === 'object' && 'type' in value && 'plurality' in value && 'source' in value) {
            const binding = value as Binding;
            
            // Add cid and property name
            binding.cid = this.cid;
            binding.property = key;
            
            console.log(`Configured binding: ${key}`, binding);
        }
    }
}
Or more defensively with a type guard:
typescript
private isBinding(value: any): value is Binding {
    return value && 
           typeof value === 'object' &&
           'type' in value &&
           'plurality' in value &&
           'source' in value &&
           typeof value.type === 'function';
}

private __configureBindings() {

type ConstructorParameters<T extends abstract new (...args: any) => any> =

It automatically returns a tuple type. When TypeScript infers P from ...args: infer P, it captures the parameter types as a tuple:
typescript

type Second = Params[1];  // number  
type Length = Params['length'];  // 3 (literal type)
The infer P in a rest parameter position ...args: infer P always produces a tuple type, not an array type. That's how TypeScript's type inference works - it preserves the exact structure of the parameters as a tuple.

Looking at React's actual children typing, the issue is that React has specific rules for how children work in components.
React's built-in children types:
ReactNode - anything renderable (includes arrays, strings, numbers, elements, null)
ReactChild - single child (string, number, or element)
ReactElement - JSX element only
PropsWithChildren<P> - adds children?: ReactNode to props
The problem with typing through constructor parameters is that React doesn't pass children as a tuple - it passes them as:
Single child: the element itself
Multiple children: an array
Array in braces: the array as a single child
Here's what actually works:
typescript
// For single required child of specific type
type $Children<T extends $Chemical> = {
    children: T extends new (child: infer C) => any ? C : never
};

// But React's JSX expects specific patterns
type ReactChildren = 
    | ReactElement  // Single element
    | string       // Text
    | number       // Number
    | Iterable<ReactNode>  // Multiple
    | ReactPortal
    | boolean
    | null
    | undefined;
The real issue: TypeScript's JSX checking has hardcoded expectations about children. When it sees a tuple type like [ReactElement], it thinks you're requiring exactly that structure, not a single element.
You might need to abandon constructor-based typing for children and use a different approach, like:
typescript
class $Child1<C = ReactNode> extends $Chemical {
    // Type stored at class level, not constructor
}
Or accept that constructor params won't map cleanly to React's children model.

The error is because TypeScript doesn't support spread types in that syntax. Here's the corrected version:
typescript
export type $Children<T extends $Chemical> = T extends new (...args: infer P) => any ? 
    P extends [] ? 
        {} :                                               // No params = no children

TypeScript can't properly handle rest parameters in conditional types like [...infer Fixed, ...Rest[]]. The spread parameters will still work at runtime, but the type system will treat them as part of the tuple.
For example:

// P will be inferred as [ReactNode, ...ReactElement[]]
// children will be typed as [ReactNode, ...ReactElement[]]
This simpler version handles:
No parameters → no children prop
Single parameter (array or not) → children: ThatType
Multiple parameters → children: [Type1, Type2, ...]
Rest parameters are captured as part of the tuple type automatically.

};

};

}> = ({ children }) => {

    return <div className="wrapper">{children}</div>;

    children: [

        React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button>
    ]
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

            <TextOnly>Hello World</TextOnly>
            <DivOnly><div>I am a div</div></DivOnly>
            <ButtonWrapper><Button label="Click" /></ButtonWrapper>
            <TwoKids>
                <div>First child</div>

            {/* <TextOnly><div>Not text</div></TextOnly> */}

            {/* <ButtonWrapper><div>Not a Button</div></ButtonWrapper> */}
            {/* <TwoKids><div>Only one child</div></TwoKids> */}
        </div>
    );
}

}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// 7. Tuple with spread - first div required, then any number of buttons
const FirstThenRest: React.FC<{ 
    children: [
        React.ReactElement<HTMLDivElement>,
        ...React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button>[]
    ]
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// 8. All same type with spread (0 or more)
const AnyButtons: React.FC<{ 
    children: React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button>[]
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// 9. Mixed types without array wrapper
const Mixed: React.FC<{ 
    children: ReactNode | ReactNode[]
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// Test component
export function Test() {
    return (
        <div>
            {/* Single button */}
            <ButtonList>
                <Button label="Single" />
            </ButtonList>

            {/* Multiple buttons without array */}
            <ButtonList>
                <Button label="One" />
                <Button label="Two" />
                <Button label="Three" />
            </ButtonList>

            {/* Tuple with spread - required div + optional buttons */}
            <FirstThenRest>
                <div>Required div</div>
                <Button label="Optional 1" />
                <Button label="Optional 2" />
            </FirstThenRest>

            {/* Just the required element */}
            <FirstThenRest>
                <div>Only required</div>
            </FirstThenRest>

            {/* Any number of buttons */}
            <AnyButtons>
                <Button label="A" />
                <Button label="B" />
                <Button label="C" />
            </AnyButtons>

            {/* Mixed content */}
            <Mixed>
                <div>A div</div>
                <Button label="A button" />
                <span>A span</span>
                Text content
                {42}
            </Mixed>

            {/* These would NOT compile - uncomment to see errors */}
            
            {/* Wrong first element in tuple */}
            {/* <FirstThenRest>
                <Button label="Should be div first" />
                <Button label="Button" />
            </FirstThenRest> */}
            
            {/* Wrong type in ButtonList */}
            {/* <ButtonList>
                <div>Not a button</div>
            </ButtonList> */}
        </div>
    );
}
The issue with React children typing is that when you pass multiple JSX elements as children, React automatically converts them to an array. So React.ReactElement[] as a children type requires an explicit array in curly braces, which isn't natural JSX.
The union type ReactElement | ReactElement[] accepts both single and multiple children naturally.
Doug
18:28 UTC, 9 September 2025
Why do you need the union type if the array works for multiple without it being nested?
Claude
18:29 UTC, 9 September 2025
You're right to question this! The issue is that React's JSX children typing is inconsistent.
When you write:
tsx
<ButtonList>
    <Button />
    <Button />
    <Button />
</ButtonList>
React passes this to the component as an array. But TypeScript's type checking for JSX is stricter - if you type children as just ReactElement[], TypeScript expects you to write:
tsx
<ButtonList>
    {[<Button />, <Button />, <Button />]}
</ButtonList>
This is a mismatch between how React works (automatically converting multiple children to an array) and how TypeScript checks JSX (requiring explicit array syntax for array-typed children).
The union type ReactElement | ReactElement[] is a workaround that makes TypeScript accept both:
Single child (passed as single element)
Multiple children (passed as array, but written without explicit array syntax)
Actually, for true "spread" behavior where you want 0 or more of the same type without explicit arrays, you'd need:
tsx
type ButtonListProps = {
    children?: React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button> | React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button>[]
}
This accepts:
No children
One Button
Multiple Buttons (without array brackets)
It's a TypeScript JSX limitation, not a React limitation.
Doug
18:31 UTC, 9 September 2025
Does that trick work for multiple types?
[Component1 | Component1[], Component2 | Component2[]]
//Does this work? <1> <1> <2>
Claude
18:31 UTC, 9 September 2025
No, that trick doesn't work for tuples with multiple types. TypeScript's JSX type checking doesn't handle position-based children well.
If you type children as:
tsx
children: [
    Component1 | Component1[], 
    Component2 | Component2[]
]
TypeScript still expects a tuple structure, and the union doesn't help with positional requirements.
For mixed types in order without array brackets, you're stuck with:
Using a single permissive type like ReactNode
Accepting that TypeScript can't enforce the order/types without explicit array syntax
Using runtime validation instead of compile-time types
The fundamental issue is that React passes multiple children as a flat array at runtime, but TypeScript's tuple types expect exact positional matching. There's no good way to type "first child must be Component1, second must be Component2" without requiring array syntax.
For your Chemistry framework with constructor-based typing:
typescript
constructor(first: Component1, second: Component2) {}
// Creates children type: [Component1, Component2]
// Requires explicit array syntax in JSX
This is a limitation where TypeScript's type system and React's JSX handling don't align well. You can have either:
Strong typing with awkward syntax (explicit arrays)
Natural syntax with weak typing (ReactNode)
But not both.
Doug
18:34 UTC, 9 September 2025
But does a spread work in the tuple type?
Claude
18:34 UTC, 9 September 2025
Yes, spreads work in tuple types for JSX children! This is actually the best solution:
tsx
// This type accepts a div followed by any number of Buttons
type SpreadChildren = [
    React.ReactElement<HTMLDivElement>,
    ...React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button>[]
];

const SpreadExample: React.FC<{ children: SpreadChildren }> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// These all work naturally:
<SpreadExample>
    <div>Required first</div>
</SpreadExample>

<SpreadExample>
    <div>Required first</div>
    <Button label="Optional" />
</SpreadExample>

<SpreadExample>
    <div>Required first</div>
    <Button label="One" />
    <Button label="Two" />
    <Button label="Three" />
</SpreadExample>
The spread in the tuple [First, ...Rest[]] tells TypeScript:
First element must be the specified type
After that, accept any number (including 0) of the Rest type
No explicit array syntax needed!
This is perfect for your constructor-based typing:
typescript
constructor(
    header: React.ReactElement<HTMLDivElement>,
    ...buttons: React.ReactElement<any, typeof Button>[]
) {}
// Generates children type: [ReactElement<HTMLDivElement>, ...ReactElement<any, typeof Button>[]]
This gives you strong typing with natural JSX syntax - exactly what you want for Chemistry!
Doug
18:36 UTC, 9 September 2025
Is there a way of typing the basic elements as strings? Like 'div"
Claude
18:36 UTC, 9 September 2025
Yes! React provides types for HTML elements using string literals:
tsx
import React from 'react';

// Using string literals for HTML elements
const DivOnly: React.FC<{ 
    children: React.ReactElement<any, 'div'>
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <section>{children}</section>;
};

const SpanOnly: React.FC<{ 
    children: React.ReactElement<any, 'span'>
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// Multiple HTML element types
const HtmlElements: React.FC<{
    children: [
        React.ReactElement<any, 'header'>,
        React.ReactElement<any, 'main'>,
        React.ReactElement<any, 'footer'>
    ]
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <div>{children}</div>;
};

// Union of string literals
const DivOrSpan: React.FC<{
    children: React.ReactElement<any, 'div' | 'span'>
}> = ({ children }) => {
    return <section>{children}</section>;
};

// Test component
export function Test() {
    return (
        <div>
            <DivOnly>
                <div>Valid div</div>
            </DivOnly>

            <SpanOnly>
                <span>Valid span</span>
            </SpanOnly>

            <HtmlElements>
                <header>Header content</header>
                <main>Main content</main>
                <footer>Footer content</footer>
            </HtmlElements>

            <DivOrSpan>
                <div>A div works</div>
            </DivOrSpan>

            <DivOrSpan>
                <span>A span works too</span>
            </DivOrSpan>

            {/* These would error */}
            {/* <DivOnly>
                <span>Not a div</span>
            </DivOnly> */}
        </div>
    );
}
The string literal types like 'div', 'span', 'header' correspond to the HTML element tag names. TypeScript knows these map to the intrinsic JSX elements.

// Updated symbolize function that handles Chemicals
function symbolize(value: any): string {
    return stringify(value, function(this: any, key: string, val: any): any {
        if (key === '') return val;
        
        // Handle Chemical instances - return their cid
        if (val instanceof $Chemical) return { _cid: val.cid };
        
        // Skip non-reactive properties when parent is Chemical
        if (this instanceof $Chemical && !isReactiveProperty(this, key, val))
            return undefined;
        
        // Skip functions
        if (typeof val === 'function') return undefined;
        
        // Handle Next.js proxies if needed
        if (val?.constructor?.name === 'Proxy') return '[Proxy]';
        
        return val;
    });
}

// Reactive decorator for methods
export function reactive() {
    return function (target: any, property: string) {
        const dynamicTarget: any = target;
        if (!dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey])
            dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey] = new DecoratorCache();
        const decorators: DecoratorCache = dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey];
        decorators.reactive.set(property, true);
    };
}

// Updated DecoratorCache to include reactive
class DecoratorCache {
    $: Map<string, { type: Type, expecting: '?' | '!' | '[]' }> = new Map();
    parent: Map<string, Type> = new Map();
    inert: Map<string, boolean> = new Map();
    dynamic: Map<string, ((value: any) => any) | undefined> = new Map();
    reactive: Map<string, boolean> = new Map();  // New!
}

// Updated isReactiveProperty to use decorator cache
function isReactiveProperty(instance: any, key: string, value: any, decorators?: DecoratorCache): boolean {
    // Skip symbols and underscore properties
    if (typeof key === 'symbol' || key.startsWith('_')) return false;
    
    // Get decorators if not passed
    if (!decorators && instance instanceof $Chemical) {
        decorators = instance[decoratorsKey];
    }
    
    // Check if marked as inert
    if (decorators?.inert.get(key)) return false;
    
    // For functions, check if marked reactive
    if (typeof value === 'function') {
        // Only reactive if explicitly marked
        return decorators?.reactive.get(key) || false;
    }
    
    // Skip standard non-reactive properties
    if (key === 'constructor' || key === 'Component' || key === 'parent' || 
        key === 'children' || key === 'elements') return false;
    
    // All other properties are reactive by default
    return true;
}

// Updated Bond.examine to handle reactive methods
private examine(target: any, mode: 'instance' | 'prototype') {
    if (mode === 'prototype') {
        const decorators = target[decoratorsKey];

        if (parentType) {
            this._type = parentType || $Chemical;
            this._isParent = true;
            this._isChemical = true;
            this._isInert = true;
            this._isSettable = false;
            return;
        }
        
        // Check inert first - if inert, skip everything else
        if (decorators.inert.get(this._property)) {
            this._isInert = true;
            return;  // Don't process inert properties further
        }
        
        // Check reactive for functions
        const value = target[this._property];
        if (typeof value === 'function') {
            if (!decorators.reactive.get(this._property)) {
                this._isInert = true;  // Non-reactive functions are inert
                return;
            }
            // Reactive function - treat as mutable
            this._isMutable = true;
            this._symbolizer = () => this._property;  // Functions use their name as symbol
        }
        
        const dynamic = decorators.dynamic.get(this._property);
        if (dynamic !== undefined) {
            this._symbolizer = dynamic || symbolize;
            this._isMutable = true;
        }
        
        const $config = decorators.$.get(this._property);
        if ($config) {
            this._type = $config.type;
            this._isProp = this._property.startsWith('$');
            this._isChemical = true;
            this._isRequired = $config.expecting === '!';
            this._isCollective = $config.expecting === '[]';
            
            if (this._isProp) {

                if (chemical$[this._property.substring(1)] === $Chemical.$set)

                else

            }
        }
    }
    
    const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, this._property);
    if (descriptor?.get && !descriptor.set) {
        this._isSettable = false;
        this._isMutable = true;
        this._symbolizer = symbolize;
    }
    
    const value = descriptor?.get ? undefined : target[this._property];
    if (value == null) return;
    
    // Handle different value types with appropriate symbolizers
    if (value instanceof $Chemical) {
        this._isChemical = true;
        this._isValue = true;
        this._isMutable = false;
        this._symbolizer = (v: any) => v?.cid || undefined;
        if (!this._type) this._type = value.constructor as Type;

    if (valueType === 'string' || valueType === 'number' || valueType === 'boolean') {

// BondEvent extends Event to handle Chemical binding
class BondEvent<T extends $Bond = any> extends Event<T, any> {
    bind(chemical: $Chemical): void {
        if (!chemical) return;
        // Subscribe to the chemical's onUpdate to propagate changes
        chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => {
            const bond = this.source;
            const value = bond.value;
            const symbol = bond.symbolizer(value);
            this.fire({ value, symbol });
        });
    }
    
    unbind(chemical: $Chemical): void {
        if (!chemical) return;
        // Remove subscription - would need to track token
        // For now, rely on chemical.onUpdate.clear() when chemical is destroyed
    }
}

// BondEvent extends Event to handle Chemical binding
class BondEvent<Source = any, Target = any> extends Event<Source, Target> {
    private subscriptions = new Map<$Chemical, number>();
    
    bind(chemical: $Chemical): void {
        if (!chemical || this.subscriptions.has(chemical)) return;
        const token = chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => this.fire());
        this.subscriptions.set(chemical, token);
    }
    
    unbind(chemical: $Chemical): void {
        if (!chemical) return;
        const token = this.subscriptions.get(chemical);
        if (token !== undefined) {
            chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(token);
            this.subscriptions.delete(chemical);
        }
    }
    
    clear() {
        this.subscriptions.forEach((token, chemical) => {
            chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(token);
        });
        this.subscriptions.clear();
        super.clear();
    }
}

        this.chemicalMap.set(chemical, subscriber);

        const subscriber = this.chemicalMap.get(chemical);
